discovery.sequenceProgress: Progress through the illustrative EEG sequence
discovery.watch: Watch the raw EEG and the one-minute DSA together.
discovery.aboutPatient: This fictional patient has early severe ARDS. The team has documented a temporary RASS −4 goal for controlled ventilation while preparing prone positioning. This is an individual scenario, not a sedation target for every patient with ARDS. No neuromuscular blockade is present during the RASS assessments.
discovery.aboutSuppression: Deep sedation and burst suppression are different observations. RASS −4 or −5 does not define an EEG pattern. Suppression is not intended in this case; specific neurological indications require their own specialist plan.
discovery.aboutSequence: The 60-second sequence is a teaching illustration, not the time course of a drug or a patient recording. The shared simulator generates the signals. Indices are hidden because the story does not establish a numerical RASS–qCON conversion. Alpha/delta activity is an example in this propofol context, not a universal target.
discovery.aboutReview: The reassessment illustrates what the team would review together. No dose or treatment interval is calculated. A frontal EEG display complements clinical assessment; it does not provide a complete neurological diagnosis or establish analgesia.
discovery.title.3: Reassess the patient and the goal.
discovery.heading.0: What can the clinical assessment tell us?
discovery.copy.0: Our focus is the brain. EEG helps us observe propofol's effect on brain activity, alongside the clinical response. Explore the bedside context, then add the EEG.
discovery.heading.1: Deep sedation does not mean burst suppression.
discovery.copy.1: This reference shows continuous alpha/delta activity. The clinical RASS is −4 in our story. EEG and the clinical score describe different aspects of the patient's state.
discovery.heading.2: Watch the quiet intervals become longer.
discovery.copy.2: The sequence develops gradually over 60 seconds. This change may occur without a different RASS score. Check signal quality, treatment timing and other causes; do not deepen sedation just to obtain a lower number.
discovery.heading.3: Same clinical score. A more continuous pattern.
discovery.copy.3: After reviewing signal quality, possible causes and the treatment plan, the team reassesses. This illustrative endpoint combines RASS −4 with continuous EEG. The display does not calculate how to get there.
discovery.label: DISCOVER EEG
discovery.noConversion: Illustrative EEG · No fixed RASS–qCON conversion
discovery.fictional: A fictional ICU case · No quiz, no timer
room.text.0: Early severe ARDS. For this patient, the team has chosen temporary deep sedation to support controlled, lung-protective ventilation. Prone positioning is being prepared.
room.text.1: For clarity, this example shows propofol alone, delivered intravenously. It does not depict a complete ICU treatment. EEG helps us observe the effect on brain activity alongside the clinical assessment.
room.text.2: No response to voice; movement to physical stimulation. There is no neuromuscular blockade in this teaching case. This assessment does not tell us whether the EEG is continuous or suppressed.
room.illustration: Illustrative ICU scene. Propofol is delivered by a separate Agilia-style syringe pump through an IV line to the patient's hand. The breathing circuit connects the mouth to the ventilator. A bedside monitor shows ECG and oxygenation traces.
room.caption: Intubated · IV propofol · Proning planned
guide.topic.0.label: Why EEG?
guide.topic.0.title: Observe the brain during sedation.
guide.topic.0.text: Propofol changes brain activity. EEG helps us observe that effect continuously, alongside the patient's clinical response. Blood pressure and ventilator behaviour remain important, but do not directly show the EEG pattern.
guide.topic.0.note: The simulator's alpha/delta example shows continuous activity. Deep sedation does not require burst suppression.

guide.topic.1.label: Why in ICU?
guide.topic.1.title: Follow a changing clinical situation.
guide.topic.1.text: The reason for sedation can change during an ICU stay. EEG and DSA can reveal changes in continuity between clinical assessments, including unexpected suppression. Interpret the pattern with signal quality, medications and the patient's condition.
guide.topic.1.note: Clinical assessment and EEG-derived indices describe different information. There is no fixed RASS-to-qCON conversion.

guide.topic.2.label: Meet Conox
guide.topic.2.title: From the sensor to the screen.
guide.topic.2.text: A disposable forehead sensor with three electrodes records the EEG. A patient cable connects it to the monitor, which brings the waveform, spectrogram and processed indices together.
guide.topic.2.note: Conox supports monitoring during anaesthesia and sedation. It is not a diagnostic EEG system, and its indices alone do not determine a drug dose.
